item.title: Our National Polarization Has Consequences
item.description:
Identity

Our National Polarization Has Consequences

Anomie results from the absence of a shared sense of values and purpose.

Posted September 21, 2026

Key points
  • The brain increases vigilance in response to a perceived sense of threat.
  • Our trust in other people and our confidence in our institutions are at an all-time low.

On this evening’s televised news all three networks emphasized (“Breaking News!”) an unprovoked knife attack in Times Square killing one person and grievously wounding another. If you read in the newspapers about this incident or others like it, the story likely ended with some variant of the Guardians’s reference to “turbulent times” or similar descriptions decrying why things currently seem so badly out of kilter.

We don’t need to coin a new word or phrase to describe the conditions that make possible such grisly events. (Two days later police shot and killed a man wielding a knife on a cable of the Brooklyn Bridge.) Anomie popularized in 1893 by sociologist Emil Durkheim refers to a “generalized state of normlessness” where there is a breakdown of social and moral rules. In such a setting, violence increases secondary to the loss of the social constraints that ordinarily keep aggressive and other negative impulses in check, the so called “cultural corset” as it was referred to during the Victorian era.

How Stable Social Structures Regulate Human Behavior

Anomie is actually a straight forward concept: Stable social structures ordinarily regulating human behavior become less powerful as determinants of how people actually behave.

For instance during times of social breakdown (extreme polarization, political corruption, general malaise, anxiety and distress) violence tends to increase among a small percentage of individuals who until their violent act had functioned non-violently. According to Durkheim this small percentage was only tenuously restrained by social expectation and easily became untethered under conditions of stress or disorganization. For this percentage only formal legal sanctions, not social expectations, have any chance of guaranteeing behavioral compliance.

At the neurobehavioral level, a stable predictable society provides a setting in which the brain functions at its best. Neural structure and function work in synchrony to enable individual predictions of probability, a sense of confidence, trust, a spirit of common purpose and cooperation, along with the ability to regulate emotions and inhibit disruptive or violent responses. Healthy networks within the brain ordinarily reduce the cognitive effort required to function healthily in daily life. But under conditions of anomie the brain’s social judgements lose clarity and conviction. Who can be trusted? What is expected of me? Most damaging, the sense of identity becomes imperiled: “Who am I really?”

When comparatively stable social conditions deteriorate, resulting in an increasing fragmented anomic world we now inhabit, seemingly random acts of violence, like the one reported on the nightly news, become increasingly frequent nationwide. How does this come about?

The Brain’s Reaction to Anomic Times: From Vigilance to Hypervigilance

First of all, during anomic times like the present, the brain, in its attempt to make sense of the world, is driven to take in as much information as possible by increasing its vigilance. You can think of the brain as a prediction machine that is always vigilantly transforming current information into predictions of what will happen next and what should be done in response. As the condition of anomie increase, the brain’s hypervigilance kicks up several notches into a state of hypervigilance.

Hypervigilance nurtures a sense of a threat combined with a decreasing ability to trust others, social withdrawal, and a general loss of the cognitive inhibition required for maintaining sustained relationships with friends, acquaintances and people in general. Such losses in social connection provoke anxiety, depression and political extremism. Currently both our trust in other people and our confidence in our institutions are at an all-time low. According to findings by the Pew Research Center, the percentage of people who believe “most people can be trusted” decreased from 34% in 1972 to 23% by 2018 and has remained at that low level since then. Another survey (Gallup 2026) found that only 27% of Americans expressed confidence in 14 of our major institutions.

Added to this are the expressions of anomie resulting from the ever burgeoning digital/ social media environment engulfing us. Although this environment connects vast numbers of us, those connections involve for the most part social voice-mediated or screen-mediated social interactions that lack the verisimilitude of one person encountering another in the flesh.

With even greater vigilance comes increases in the perception of subjectively threatening information that acts as a multiplier resulting in greater vigilance and stress. Under such conditions of uncertainty and threat, people holding similar views tend to attract one another and form groups. Shared explanations, even erroneous ones—in fact, especially erroneous ones since they’re often very difficult to prove mistaken—reduce the amount and intensity of personal anxiety “Whew! So I’m not the only one who believes this”. Thanks to the accompanying reduction of anxiety, self-identity merges with the newly acquired group identity. The stronger the affiliation within the new group, the more shared-group-identity plays the predominant role: Protecting the group becomes synonymous with protecting the self. Put another way, when the larger social world becomes less intelligible, a smaller narrowly defined group becomes more and more psychologically attractive, simply because such groups tell individuals who they are and how they should think and behave.

Political Affiliation During Anomie

Both cultural history and neuroscience research demonstrate that political affiliation can become an anchoring point for self-identity. This is one of the reasons that the formation and acceptance of new political convictions is often experienced as a change in identity, not just a change in beliefs and expressed opinions. Typically the converted speak of having become a “new man” or a “new woman”. Currently we are experiencing these changes in the form of political and cultural polarization marked by many strongly held beliefs, but few shared norms. If the polarization becomes strong enough, the conflicts threaten to preclude resolution. While this process can be reversed, reversal doesn’t come easily.

Now, less than two months before the mid-term elections, let’s hope that both parties are working towards decreasing the suffocating effects of our nation’s sense of polarization that disunites us. Failure to do so, will only lead to additional polarization—the lynchpin of anomie.

Richard M. Restak, M.D.

item.title: Sex Dreams: What Your Unconscious Is Trying To Tell You
item.description:
Dreaming

Sex Dreams: What Your Unconscious Is Trying To Tell You

Erotic dreams can be a window into how we're doing sexually, relationally, and psychologically.

Posted September 21, 2026

Key points
  • Sexual dreams are nearly universal.
  • Depth psychology treats sexual dream content as meaningful and not as random noise to be explained away.
  • Approached with curiosity instead of shame, sexual dreams can become a doorway to self-knowledge.
Source: Photo by Christian Buehner on Unsplash

We spend approximately a third of our lives asleep, presuming we don't have a sleep-related health condition.1 Whether we remember it or not, we dream every night; even people who insist they never dream show the physiological signatures of dreaming when sleep researchers observe them sleep.2

Among the dreams we can remember and recall, few themes are as universal, or as avoided in conversation, as the sexual ones. One recent study found that 95 percent of research participants reported having sexual and erotic dreams.3 Interestingly, people with more frequent sexual encounters, higher relationship satisfaction, and greater sexual desire tended to dream of their current partner, while those in shorter or less satisfying relationships were more likely to dream of an ex. So, apparently your unconscious has a type.

Sexual dreams, in other words, aren't just random noise. These dreams can be a window into how we're doing relationally, sexually, and psychologically.

Why Therapists Care About Sex Dreams

More people are talking to their therapists about sex than popular culture gives us credit for, including psychodynamic, Jungian, and depth-oriented clinicians who take dream material seriously. It's easy to dismiss this as outdated psychoanalytical territory, but the field has moved well past Freud's more speculative claims. The idea of an unconscious mental life isn't controversial anymore, with thousands of psychological studies confirming we think and feel outside conscious awareness.4

What Freud assessed correctly, and what modern psychodynamic theory retains, is that a great deal of our sexual life runs within the unconscious. As a result, a sexual dream can function as a kind of self-portrait, quietly working something out without our ego's permission and editorial input.

Carl Jung took a more symbolic view of dreams, perceiving dreams to be little hidden doors into different areas of the psyche, and interpreted sexual imagery less literally than Freud.5 For instance, a dream of sexual union might be less about an erotic wish and more about two energies within a person needing psychological integration. Alternatively, a dream of masturbation might echo mythological ideas of self-becoming going back as far as Egyptian symbolism. Jung's method asks us to work a dream from multiple angles at once; to consider personal associations, life context, and the broader cultural or mythological meanings a symbol carries. Jung often encouraged his analysands to prioritize an ongoing internal conversation and to try to develop an active relationship with the symbol itself.

Source: Photo by Alex Azabache on Unsplash

Depth psychology asks us to stay curious rather than explain the dream away, feeling into its full experience before analyzing it. That felt sense is often the point, and letting our feeling world be transformed by an internal image or experience can help correct an inflated unconscious attitude, or even practically help us tend to a relationship differently. For a century, psychoanalysts and therapists have witnessed this firsthand, watching dreams help clients in ways their rational, waking minds never could have found alone.

A Culture That Doesn't Know What to Do with Dreams

Some clients in my clinical private practice struggle to sit with their dreams at all. This is because many of us were raised to treat dreams as meaningless, as "just a dream," which leaves little practice in taking our imaginal and inner life seriously.6

Add an industrial Westernized culture that prioritizes being in control, rational, and endlessly productive, and a sexual dream can land as shameful or a waste of time rather than as essential information for the human soul. Even in a culture that doesn't often know what to do with these sexually charged dreams, I've nonetheless seen how they reach further than a single night's imagery for my clients, and often surfacing waking concerns about integration or harmony, echoing past sexual trauma, or even reflecting ancient attachment patterns from early relationships that may be relevant for the dreamer to know.

A sexual dream, met with curiosity rather than judgment, is often the psyche pointing at something worth understanding; connection, desire, grief, vitality, an old wound, or energy that hasn't found anywhere else to go. Approached in a brave, unhurried space, sexual dreams can become a doorway to self-knowledge and closer relationships rather than a source of shame or embarrassment.

If this topic interests you, I recently wrote a longer academic entry on sexual dreams for the Elgar Encyclopedia of Sex and Society.7

item.title: Smart People, Poor Decisions: The Blind Spot of Success
item.description:
Decision-Making

Smart People, Poor Decisions: The Blind Spot of Success

A good track record doesn't always mean good judgment.

Posted September 21, 2026

Key points
  • Successful people may be more likely to rely on their record than current inputs when making decisions.
  • Confirmation bias and other dynamics can make us look for data that support the view we already have.
  • Being aware of our bias, and being deliberate about decisions, can push us to see counterarguments clearly.
Source: Unsplash/Vitaly Gariev

Successful people who are early in their careers and successful people who are very experienced obviously have different perspectives on how they approach their professional choices. But where they are perhaps most alike is a shared vulnerability: They both can have a hard time separating a good record from good judgment.

When those things collide people can slide into confirmation bias. A good record means things have gone your way a lot of the time. Good judgment could be the reason. The problem is assuming it’s the only reason. After decades of working with leadership teams I can say it happens with very smart people, relatively often.

Successful people are often “smart,” which I use in the simple sense of able to synthesize information rapidly. If you can process faster, it doesn’t mean you process better. In fact, if you are processing quickly but not slowing down to consider your own biases, you can race past the very thing that would give you better judgment. People who have failed in significant ways have learned the lesson of slowing down and reading the board more carefully. That can be a true gift.

Why do people with good records sometimes show shockingly poor judgment?

For people with less experience, an early amount of success can begin to feel like proof of good judgment. And it might be – there’s no reason to second-guess a whole record of good outcomes professionally or academically. But people also get lucky, or have good timing, or other structural advantages that contributed to their accomplishments. That’s true of everyone, but when you have a lot of success, and you’re still pretty early in your career, you can begin to have narratives like, “I’ve gotten every promotion I ever tried for.” Well, if you’ve been working for five years that’s less telling than if you’ve been working for thirty.

The other extreme, however, is people who do have decades of experience. For them, the likely risk is they have now been surrounded by people who want to confirm their beliefs. To say it more plainly: If you’ve done well enough over decades to be in a senior role, a lot of people probably tell you what you want to hear. You have influence over other people’s careers and ambitions, and most people generally want to please people with more power than themselves. Even though your record by now is likely more “flawed” than someone with five years of experience, you can end up equally convinced of your own view as the right one.

For the person who is early in their career, the poor judgment can be a useful life lesson. The sooner they stop relying on a good track record, the sooner they can use actual judgment to make sure their reasons are sound, instead of mere historical confidence. For those at the experienced level, learning to reflect more thoughtfully can require more proactive awareness.

Better judgment comes with deliberation, not doubt

The answer is not to become paralyzed with doubt. That becomes a judgment about yourself. It is to feel more fully informed. Then, deliberation is a judgment about the decision. Stay confident that you can understand and consider all the inputs. At the same time, push yourself to see information that works against your assumptions.

Overconfidence comes from history-based certainty in your view because you’ve been successful, consider yourself smart, or generally have a good record. Informed confidence comes from being willing to look at the current situation with an open mind and take on evidence counter to what you believe to be true. Think of the annoying person who likes to play devil’s advocate. It’s irritating. But once you’ve had to lay out your argument and defeat all challenges, you generally feel even more certain.

How to test your rationality, without doubting your intelligence

It can be genuinely unnerving to start examining your biases. We all do it, to a certain degree. In a professional capacity, one way to test your rationality is to think about a belief or decision that you are confident in. When is the last time you’ve actively looked for evidence that you are wrong? Why?

Test yourself with any straightforward work decision: Do you always choose the same person to manage a project? When was the last time you asked someone else? Or, who do you turn to at work for advice? When was the last time you asked someone else? It’s not about blowing up relationships or processes. It’s simply being aware of what decisions you make as you speed along with unchecked confidence, and which decisions are built on confidence earned as you processed the situation. No one gets it right all the time. That shouldn’t signal a loss in confidence, but rather smarter decision making.

item.title: Born Under the Gaslight: Five Steps to Heal
item.description:
Gaslighting

Born Under the Gaslight: Five Steps to Heal

How to reject the lie and start living in the truth.

Posted September 21, 2026

Key points
  • Growing up with messages that contradict reality teaches you to distrust your own perceptions.
  • Gaslighting and emotional neglect often come from the same parent, in the same moment.
  • The problem was never that something is wrong with you. The problem belongs to your childhood.
  • Trusting your own feelings again can be learned, and trust is the foundation of everything.
Source: StockAdobe/DimaBerlin

Fourteen-year-old Olivia sits at the dinner table with her family, picking at her food. While the others talk in the background, she is absorbed in her own thoughts, trying to sort out in her head why her math teacher seems to hate her. "Why don't teachers like me? I try so hard, but I must be doing something wrong that I don't know about," she worries for the six hundredth time.

"Olivia!" her father says suddenly, breaking through her reverie. "When your mother talks, you listen!" Startled and overwhelmed in the moment, tears come to Olivia's eyes. "There you go again," her mother says. "You don't even bother to listen when I talk, and then you pull out the tears. I've never seen such a selfish kid."

Olivia has been called selfish many times by her parents. They use this word often when they are not happy with something that she did or said or felt. In reality, Olivia is anything but selfish. She is by nature a kind and caring child. She worries a lot, and she feels things deeply. She keeps it all inside because she knows that there is not room for her worries and feelings and problems in her childhood home.

As Olivia goes forward with her life, grows into a young adult, and then gets married and has children herself, she will be troubled by a contradiction that she can't resolve. Deep down, she knows that she's not selfish. But she was labeled that way at every turn by the people who are supposed to love and care for her most: her parents.

As a psychologist who has specialized in childhood emotional neglect for years, I have seen how long that contradiction can last, and how quietly it does its work.

In an earlier post, I described the different forms this takes in a family. Growing up with messages that contradict each other, and/or contradict reality, you grow up walking on shaky ground, unable to trust yourself, your world, or the people around you, and feeling deeply invalid and alone.

What Else Was Happening

There is a name for the other half of what happened to Olivia. Her parents not only told her she was something she was not. They also failed to notice who she actually was.

That is childhood emotional neglect. It’s not about what your parents did to you. It’s about what your parents didn’t do for you.

article continues after advertisement

A parent who overrides your feelings is not paying attention to them either. So the gaslighting and the neglect come from the same parent, in the same moment, and the second one is even harder to see than the first.

Is the gaslight effect a life sentence? How can a child like Olivia, once grown, get her feet back on the firm, solid surface of the Earth? How can she learn to trust herself? How can she realize that she's not crazy?

There are eight billion people on the Earth, and no two childhood experiences are the same. Everyone born under the gaslight takes with them their own unique set of challenges. But there are some particular steps that you can take to move yourself toward health, strength, self-confidence, and happiness.

How to Get Your Feet Back on the Ground

  1. Tune Into Yourself. As a child, you were taught that your perceptions and feelings were wrong, but it's not true. Now you will have to fully accept that you're not crazy, and that your feelings and perceptions are not only valid, but have value. Pay attention to yourself.
  2. Learn and Practice Meditation or Mindfulness. Mindfulness is helpful for many emotional issues (Goldberg et al., 2022). But here it offers an extra bonus. It will not only help you focus your attention inward to accomplish the first step, it will also help you to ground yourself. If you're riddled by self-doubt, question the reliability of your own perceptions, and if you are out of touch with your own feelings, mindfulness can help. The mindfulness skill allows you to focus your attention inward whenever you need to check in with yourself.
  3. Accept That You're Not Flawed. You've spent much of your life wondering about yourself. What's wrong with me? Or maybe even, "Am I crazy?" Now it's time for you to let go of that. Put the real problem in its actual place: your childhood.
  4. Start Trusting Yourself. No matter how strong your feelings are, they are there for a reason, and they make sense. Your perceptions are real, and they matter. Stop believing the gaslighting, and trust yourself and your feelings instead.
  5. Reach Out For Help. It's difficult to do this kind of recovery all alone. Did others make you think that reaching out is wrong? Guess what. They are wrong. Talk to a friend or family member who has a proven history of trustworthiness. Or find a trained mental health professional who you feel you can trust. Then talk to that person, and let them be your guide as you walk away, farther and farther from the gaslight and toward your own inner truth and light.

Healing from the gaslight is a special challenge, mostly because it's hard to trust yourself (and maybe others too). And trust is the foundation of everything.

Living in the Truth

Essentially, living under the gaslight is like living under a lie. The lie is, "The world doesn't make sense." The truth is, the world does make sense. And you make sense if you only start to understand yourself.

article continues after advertisement

So now, it's your turn. It's your time to shine. Do the work, and you'll feel your feet meeting the ground. You'll feel the warmth of your own emotions and your own reality.

You'll be living in the truth, not the lie.

To find a therapist, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

A version of this post also appears on emotionalneglect.com

© Jonice Webb, Ph.D.

item.title: AI Helps DraftKings to Exploit the Most Vulnerable Gamblers
item.description:
Ethics and Morality

AI Helps DraftKings to Exploit the Most Vulnerable Gamblers

Marketing promotions entice gamblers to keep betting.

Posted September 21, 2026

Key points
  • DraftKings uses AI to identify who is betting in a risky manner and then targets them with promotions.
  • Following the alcohol and tobacco industries, the gambling industry embraces “personal responsibility."
  • The betting apps are designed to telescope a person’s world to the apps alone.
  • DraftKings shelved the development of an AI model that could predict those who might develop an addiction.

A story in The New York Times has revealed a new predatory use of Artificial Intelligence (AI). DraftKings, one of the biggest online sports betting companies, uses AI to target those people who have some of the steepest losses or longest times spent on its platforms. Originally designed to measure how well its various target marketing strategies and promotions worked, DraftKings’ AI models quickly discovered that those people who lost the most were more likely to respond to marketing and promotions.

In other words, DraftKings raises its profit by targeting those who may or already have developed a gambling addiction. On a purely economic model that maximizes profit, it makes good business sense for online betting companies to target the most vulnerable.

On a moral level, it is deeply exploitative and reinscribes the view that people struggling with addiction are moral failures or lack willpower.

How does exploitation work?

The marketing and promotion offers are varied. Some are for “bonus” money that a player can use for “free” wagers. The “free” part stems from the money coming from the house; a person is not spending his own money.

Others involve spending $5.00 and receiving $200.00 credit spread over several days. Others are promotions for a 50% profit boost on some bets. Yet others are for a share of $2,000,000.00 if your player scores the first touchdown in the 1:00 Sunday NFL games.

Jacob Shulkin, a DraftKings data scientist, knows exactly why the promotions are so effective with those who are losing the most. Taking advantage of a gambler’s psychology is straightforward. As he notes, “I feel like I’m getting free money, but really it’s dragging me back in.” The $5.00 from the promotion was free, but all the money that follows is most surely not.

“Personal responsibility”

The philosopher Wittgenstein once noted that the decisive movement in a conjuring trick is the one that seems quite innocent. When it comes to addiction, that “innocent” move is that addiction is solely a function of individual choices. After all, it is individuals who gamble. This is where the model of “personal responsibility” gets its teeth.

The gambling industry has embraced the “personal responsibility” model of gambling, following the playbook of the alcohol and tobacco industries. Like them, the gambling industry places the onus and all responsibility on individuals and their choices. Any suffering a person experiences or inflicts on others is solely a consequence of bad choices, lack of willpower, impulsivity, weak moral character, or even bad luck.

Design shapes the choices and behaviors of people. The gambling industry figured out early that a key to success was in the design of the physical spaces. With neither clocks nor windows but plenty of flashing lights and sounds from various tables and machines with irregular payouts, along with copious supplies of alcohol and nicotine (until non-smoking regulations took effect), casinos separate a gambler from his usual world. Or put differently, the world is reduced to the casino.

With online gambling, the world is reduced to apps on a person’s telephone or computer. Those apps have many different lights, sounds, advertisements, promotions, and deals. All of those fragment a person’s attention from other parts of their life, while at the same time producing hyper- or telescoped focus on the app. All of this encourages people gambling to stay engaged for much longer stretches of time.

In the gambling industry, warnings abound about responsible playing but not gambling. Betting is playing, which are two very different things for many people. DraftKings offers 10 principles to help people play responsibly. Among them:

  • wagers should be for entertainment purposes only
  • don’t chase losses
  • set realistic limits and don’t play beyond them
  • don’t view gaming as a pathway for financial success

DraftKings also has a Responsible Gaming Center, where a person can set various alarms for themselves, track their wagering history, impose limits on time or types of play, and manage their payment histories. Players can also take a time-out or have a cool-off period for a set amount of time and put themselves on self-exclusion lists.

Since one must be logged into their DraftKings account to use any of these features, it isn’t hard to imagine that these features are among the most closely monitored by DraftKings. The prime candidates for marketing and promotions are those who impose limits and remove them repeatedly.

Could AI help to predict problem gamblers?

DraftKings did, for a short amount of time, develop an AI model that would help the Responsible Gaming Division to identify gamblers who were demonstrating risky behavior. The designer of the model, Nestor Hernandez, wanted to harness its predictive power. As he noted, “the idea of this model is to be more proactive instead of being reactive…You will basically predict that a user will be in trouble, let’s say a few days or a few weeks in advance. And you can act accordingly.”

Though this model used the same sort of data about betting patterns as the one used for promotional marketing, research for it and related models was discontinued. The reason offered was that it was not evidence-based.

Allowing that model to run would be a tacit acknowledgment that DraftKings has some responsibilities to its customers. That acknowledgment, however, would be contrary to the personal responsibility model that dominates the gambling universe.

Lawsuits came for Big Tobacco. Lawsuits are coming for Big Social Media. It may be only a matter of time before lawsuits start coming for Big Betting.

item.title: Back to School, Back to Play
item.description:
Play

Back to School, Back to Play

Early childhood educators speak out about play's value in everyday school life

Posted September 21, 2026

Key points
  • Play has been shown to have a large number of benefits, for both socioemotional and academic learning.
  • However, play time is consistently being reduced in schools.
  • As children return to school, three elementary teachers weigh in on the importance of play each school day.

As I have discussed in previous blogs, teachers, parents, and children all appreciate the benefits of play while at school. However, the amount of time allotted for play in schools has decreased in recent years (Russ & Dillon, 2011) (see also the Playtime Matters Report). For example, a 2010 survey of 1,951 schools showed that half reported having recess periods of 30 minutes or less each day (Russ & Dillon, 2011).

Research supporting the inclusion of both structured and unstructured play in school curricula has consistently shown positive results (e.g., Dearbury & Jones, 2020) When children engage in structured play, they practice following directions, taking turns, cooperating, problem-solving, memory, social skills, language development, and self-regulation. During unstructured play, children practice sharing, problem-solving, creativity, organization, negotiation, time management, patience, empathy, self-regulation, how to win and lose, how to make and correct mistakes, recognizing strengths and weakness in self and others, and physical movement and coordination.

Source: Katherine Hanlon/ Unsplash

Several studies have illuminated the benefits of play-based learning (PBL) in the classroom. For example, Blinkoff and colleagues (2024) examined the effects of an intervention designed to help kindergarten teachers transition to a play-based kindergarten mandate in the state of New Hampshire. After the intervention, students were more engaged with learning, more active in their use of learning tools, and more communicative.

Similarly, Scott et al. (2025) found that preschoolers from disadvantaged backgrounds (who are often at risk for lower vocabulary) learned just as many new words in a playful learning context as they did in shared book reading, with effects persisting 4 ½ months later. Hui et al. (2015) illustrated how infusing creative arts and playfulness into early childhood curricula enhanced children’s creative performances and overall creativity. Blinkoff et al. (2023) and Hirsh-Pasek et al. (2022) noted a link between playful learning and classroom success in the areas of collaboration, communication, content, critical thinking, creative innovation, and confidence.

One possible barrier to early childhood educators incorporating PBL into their classrooms is the need for assessment. For example, Barblett et al. (2016) reported that Western Australian early years educators described their most significant concern as the erosion of play-based learning, and tensions over whether it was a legitimate pedagogical tool. Jachyra & Fusco (2014) also noted that early childhood educators, students, and assistants find it difficult to balance the inclusion of play-based curricula with standardized testing. Taylor & Boyer (2019) similarly described the challenge of integrating important academic standards and developmentally appropriate learning experiences (such as PBL) into the kindergarten classroom, noting that teachers need support in order to implement and assess PBL strategies.

What Teachers Think About the Power of Play

In an effort to learn from current early childhood educators the extent to which they value play in their classrooms, I interviewed three school teachers (two kindergarten teachers and one ESL teacher who has worked with children ranging in age from kindergarten to third grade). These teachers work at a mid-sized suburban school with students who are both socioeconomically and ethnically diverse. Class sizes in the lower grades range from about 16-22. I will summarize their views below.

First, I asked the teachers how important they believe play to be in the daily lives of children in the age group with which they work. All three of the teachers said they believed play to be incredibly important, and all mentioned that children learn through play. One teacher reflected that this learning is “just as valuable as the academic work we do with students.” As with the work cited above, the teachers referenced skills gained through play including following directions, taking turns, cooperating, teamwork, negotiation, problem-solving, conflict resolution, and early math concepts.

Source: Rewired Digital/ Unsplash

Due to the diversity of children that these teachers work with, more than one of them highlighted the usefulness of play for developing language and communication skills. The ESL teacher noted that play “gives them the opportunity to interact with their peers in a low-stress, natural environment where they feel more comfortable taking linguistic risks. I often find that students are much more willing to use and experiment with English during [play]…[The relationships developed during play] can carry over into the classroom, helping students feel more comfortable participating in academic discussions, collaborating with peers and engaging in teamwork throughout the school day.”

One of the kindergarten teachers agreed, stating, “Most of my students are multi-language learners who are learning English as their second (or more) language. Playing allows them to interact with others while learning vocabulary as well.”

I next asked the teachers if they believed that play should have a role in the daily school days of the children they work with. Although they stated that children in their school are only allotted 20 minutes of recess a day, they all agreed that play is valuable and can and should be incorporated into the classroom as well. One kindergarten teacher said, “By having different types of play throughout the day, children are able to practice different skills. They can use team building, problem solving, creative imagination, all in different ways. By playing in the classroom, students are able to do all of these things while bringing lessons to life in a meaningful way.”

Source: Husniati Salma/ Unsplash

Additionally, I asked the teachers whether they noticed a difference in the children they work with before versus after play periods. The teachers described their students as being more “refreshed,” more ready to learn, “happier,” “rejuvenated,” “more energetic,” “reset,” and “more focused” after play.

Finally, I asked them if there as anything about the specific needs of the children they work with that makes pay particularly important. Once again, the ESL teacher noted the value of play for practicing language and communication for her students:

“Play is also valuable because it helps multilingual students build relationships and develop a sense of belonging… Even when my students are brand new to learning English, they are still able to engage in play with their classmates… Through shared materials, actions, gestures, and imagination, children find ways to communicate and participate together… [P]lay creates opportunities for connection and communication that go beyond language.”

Source: Megan Watson/ Unsplash

The kindergarten teachers agreed, noting that “play [is] important for all students with all needs. The great thing about play is that it can be tailored to meet any child's needs!”

In sum, the teachers all clearly agreed upon the value of play in early childhood education. As children and teachers return to school this fall, let us hope that play can be incorporated more regularly into the school day—for everyone’s sake!

item.title: The Downside of Being Good at Everything
item.description:
Stress

The Downside of Being Good at Everything

Why your brain needs you to stop making everything easier.

Posted September 21, 2026

Key points
  • Not all stress is bad stress when it comes to your brain.
  • The drive to be good at everything could be why you're procrastinating.
  • Sometimes stress is a response to doing something that matters to us.

Rachel Entrekin ran for 56 hours, 9 minutes, and 48 seconds to win the Cocodona 250. An ultramarathon through Arizona. She stopped three times for what she called “dirt naps,” where she lay down in the dirt, slept for 5-7 minutes, then got up and kept running. She set a course record. Beating every other woman and man.

Why can Rachel Entrekin run for over 2.5 days and I can barely make it three blocks before I’m breathing so hard that my smartwatch tells me to sit down?

Yes, she’s more experienced than me. Yes, she’s practiced. Yes, there are probably 453 other reasons why Rachel is a better runner than I am.

But that’s not why I love her story as a neuropsychologist who’s spent the past decade helping high-achieving women understand why hard work stops working.

Running for 56 hours is hard. Really freaking hard. No matter how many years you’ve spent training.

The women in leadership I work with already know how to work hard. In fact, they’ve become experts at making hard work look easy. And that’s the problem. For your brain, your body, and your business.

Easy hard versus hard hard

When we think of perfectionists, we think of someone like Monica from "Friends." Those of us who label our craft closet. And re-read this post 57 times to make sure there are zero typos.

When I’m planning my family’s summer camps and I print out a calendar with color-coded pick-up and drop-off times for each camp, we recognize this type of perfectionism.

But let’s be honest; it works.

That type of hard work is how I built my business. By being the one who keeps everything organized and on track. And you probably built your career that way, too.

The problem is there’s another way that perfectionism shows up for high achievers. It’s easy to miss.

Running for me activates this second type of perfectionism.

Jogging is stressful for me. Even thinking about jogging makes me want to procrastinate. I will voluntarily wash my kitchen floors before I will go on a jog. Because I know I’m not good at it.

Because we’re hard workers, our gold-star-collecting brains procrastinate on the hard work where we might not be good enough.

The hard work we know how to do?

  • Answering 47 emails in the 5 minutes between back-to-back meetings
  • Managing everyone else's priorities so nothing gets missed
  • Perfecting a presentation you’ve already given 10 times

Yes, this is hard. It’s why you’re exhausted at the end of the day. But this is hard you know you’re good at. So we get sucked into this busywork spiral.

The hard work your brain is less certain of?

  • Writing the first terrible draft of an article
  • Pitching yourself for a keynote you’ve never delivered
  • Making a decision on a new offer when you don’t know if it will work

That kind of hard feels wildly uncomfortable for our brains.

So our inner perfectionist avoids. It procrastinates.

Because we’ve become so good at making the hard work look easy, our brains put up walls when we try to do things that we might not be good at.

But that same inner drive to be good at everything is what’s burning us out.

Because you don't have to be good at something for it to be good for you.

Not all stress is bad stress

Most of us agree public speaking is stressful. I love presenting. I do it regularly. But Google my TEDx talk. My voice is shaking like it’s the first time I ever stepped on a stage. Because it’s stressful to get up in front of a group of people and talk.

Turns out, what your brain believes about that stress matters more than the stress itself.

You’ve probably heard chronic stress is bad. Headaches, heart disease, high blood pressure, sleep issues, weight gain, and even memory issues are all linked to this kind of stress.

But a research team at Yale led by Alia Crum showed it’s not that simple.

They evaluated whether participants had a “stress-is-enhancing” or “stress-is-debilitating” mindset.

When we see stress as debilitating, we avoid. We procrastinate on making that call to a client because we know it’s going to be super awkward, and we don’t want to have the conversation.

Individuals who see stress as enhancing don’t ignore stress; they don’t minimize it, but they see it as something that could make them better in the long run.

And when it comes to your brain, how you think about stress matters.

The team at Yale told participants they had 10 minutes to prep to speak in front of the class, and they would be evaluated by a group of experts. Then they were given a choice about whether or not they wanted to hear feedback.

People who naturally viewed stress as enhancing were more likely to ask for feedback. Which is a good thing, because feedback is stressful but critical to us growing in business and in life.

We know chronic stress can be harmful. But we've started treating all stress as something we should avoid. As if the goal is to create a life where nothing feels difficult, uncomfortable, or overwhelming.

Stress isn't always a sign that something is wrong. Sometimes it's a response to doing something that matters to us.

What if being bad at something is exactly what you need?

I've been back to jogging for three months now. And I still suck.

I haven't magically transformed into Rachel Entrekin. I'm not signing up for an ultramarathon. I'm not even interested in running a 10K.

But I've started approaching it differently. I don't need to make every experience more efficient, more productive, or more successful. Sometimes I can just do something because it's hard.

Rachel Entrekin knows that. It’s why she can hit the pain wall running for almost 3 days and only need a dirt nap.

I’m learning it. With a 30-minute jog that’s more of a jog-walk around my block.

The goal isn’t to get better at jogging. The goal is to remind my brain that doing something hard is worth it.

item.title: The Unexpected Cost of Learning About Yourself
item.description:
Wisdom

The Unexpected Cost of Learning About Yourself

The road to self-knowledge is bumpy.

Posted September 21, 2026

Key points
  • Self-knowledge is an important part of development.
  • Learning about yourself can be challenging.
  • Development involves acknowledging and accepting the unappealing parts of yourself.
Source: Ahmetatak/Pexels

I recently published a paper that presents a model of personal and professional development focused on gaining self-knowledge. Implicit in the model is that acquiring self-knowledge is beneficial and should lead to desirable outcomes such as wisdom, well-being and psychological adjustment.

However, another paper just came out demonstrating that self-knowledge is virtually unrelated to psychological adjustment. The authors of the article defined adjustment as “adaptive functioning in personal and social life” and after reviewing the available research, concluded that “the results do not support the idea that self-knowledge, in its various contents and types, is a general predictor of well-being or interpersonal functioning.”

How do we square this circle? It seems almost obvious that self-knowledge will help us thrive both personally and interpersonally. For example, as we grow older we tend to learn more about our individual strengths, weaknesses, and behavioral tendencies. As we come to recognize and accept these aspects of ourselves, we are clearly in a position to make better decisions about things like selecting jobs and activities we will find fulfilling, and tailoring our behaviour to promote successful social interactions. This should promote well-being and adjustment—shouldn’t it?

At least part of the answer may lie in a piece of the puzzle that possibly escaped your attention above: acceptance.

Full self-knowledge includes gaining insight into the aspects of ourselves we may find unappealing, such as the fact that we may be selfish, boastful, or cowardly. This can be a tough pill to swallow. Decades of research has shown that people tend to think overly positively about themselves. Accepting negative qualities is difficult. But accepting the bad along with the good may be a vital part of growth and a necessary ingredient in developing the wisdom that supports “the good life” including well-being and healthy adjustment.

As the wisdom researchers Nic Westrate and Judith Glück suggest, “wise people… see life in deep, complex, and realistic terms. Several wisdom conceptions assume that wise individuals are more aware of the dark sides of human life than others.” Wise people do not shy away from reflecting on challenging aspects of life, including the unattractive side of themselves, which helps them become better at handling problems and crises. Certainly this should promote development, maturity and psychological adjustment.

If we view the story of the relationship between self-knowledge and desirable outcomes as a movie instead of a photograph we can better appreciate the developmental flow of events in which a dip in desirable qualities such as well-being may be a necessary first step on the path to enhanced adjustment. We often must struggle through the uneasiness of accepting our shortcomings before we learn to become comfortable with them. Put another way, we need to wrestle with our demons before we can dance with our angels. The road to self-knowledge is bumpy.

This is something I highlight in my paper. I note that development can produce “outcomes that are not immediately desirable, such as fear, depression, or anxiety. Indeed, research reveals that the process of meditation, in which meditators often open themselves to the darker side of themselves, often produces negative outcomes. This may be a necessary step on the path to self-knowledge.”

So, self-knowledge may indeed be related to psychological adjustment, but that adjustment may be a longer-term outcome of a process that includes short-term challenges that can reflect maladjustment. This process, which unfolds over time, may be masked by the “snapshots” that tend to characterize psychological research on the topic. Also, the relationship between self-knowledge and desirable outcomes may be restricted to people who are willing to confront and accept those aspects of themselves they find unappealing or even frightening. It’s also possible that the way we conceptualize and measure self-knowledge and adjustment needs some fine tuning.

The desire for self-knowledge is as old as time. But the process is not straightforward or easy. If it were, most self-help books would be unnecessary. Personal and professional development can be tough, stressful, and scary. But, in the end, learning who we really are, and who we can become, may be one of the most important quests we can undertake.

item.title: How to Stop Traumatic Memories Blocking Grief
item.description:
Trauma

How to Stop Traumatic Memories Blocking Grief

A powerful way to neutralise traumatic memories that are preventing grieving.

Posted September 21, 2026

Key points
  • Emotionally charged memories of traumatic loss can make it hard to move beyond them.
  • Traumatic memories block the opportunity for the normal grief and sadness that lead gradually to healing.
  • Human givens therapists deal effectively with the trauma memories first.
Source: Claudia Wolff / Unsplash

A book I am reading made me momentarily very sad. Not the book itself or the subject matter, which is very thought-provoking. It’s called The Hidden Power of Questions in a World That Wants Answers by philosopher Lani Watson.1 Watson recalls going to see her therapist, explaining, “I had begun attending therapy, not for the first or last time, to work through a traumatic experience from my late teens in which I had lost a treasured friend in unthinkable and unbearable circumstances.”

The therapist asked: “What is one thing that you can’t do now that you want to be able to do in the future?” Watson recognised later that the question could have taken her in many directions but that she understood it in terms of how she wanted things to be different as a result of the therapy. She thought about it and replied that she wished to be able to put a photo of her friend by her bed and smile when she saw it.

She continued with the therapy for another year, exploring the associated painful thoughts and feelings, and went on to comment in her book, "Yes, I do want to have a picture of my friend on my bedside (I still don’t) … but [the question] was an opportunity to reflect on why I was there and how I wanted or needed things to change.”

It is no surprise to me, as a human givens therapist, that how we ask questions is often key to transformations, but what made me sad was that Watson has seemingly remained traumatised for so long by the circumstances of her friend’s tragic death.

The Rewind Technique

Human givens therapists are trained in a refined version of the rewind technique,2 a noninvasive method of neutralising persistent, disabling high emotional arousal associated with trauma, reactivated any time a reminder is triggered. The method is extremely powerful and is carried out with the client in a state of deep relaxation, to avoid any risk of retraumatisation. Although it will not help everyone (nothing helps everyone), we have extremely high success rates, usually in just one session.

What I mean by "one session" is that, by the end of that session, when successful, the traumatic event has been converted into a narrative memory of something still deeply sad or tragic but no longer emotionally overwhelming. The technique does not magic away feelings and beliefs that are held about the event or its circumstances, and that is why, in human givens training, it is stressed that the rewind technique is not a standalone technique but must always be just one tool within an overall focus on helping clients recover and go on to meet their needs effectively.

I once saw a client whose partner had died in a horrific road traffic accident that was none of his making. They were due to get married in three weeks. She came to see me over a year after the tragedy, as she was still struggling to function or find pleasure in anything. We were able to use the rewind technique successfully to neutralise the high emotion still associated with her partner’s death, eliminating the almost constant triggers that floored her.

This enabled her to start to grieve him in a calmer way, without the constant intrusion of the horror scenario that she had imagined, and truly to come to terms not only with his loss but also the loss of their future together. I encouraged her to choose a way to celebrate him—she chose to light a candle once a week and think about what they had shared together. But I have had other clients who did, indeed, want to have a photo by the bed or elsewhere in the house and be able to feel pleasure in seeing it.

Most importantly, in the case of this client, we used guided imagery as a means for her to imagine moving forward, always keeping a place for her lost partner in her heart (visualising herself lighting that candle for as long as she needed to), recognising what he would want for her and rehearsing ways that she could open up her life again. In the safe space of the therapy room, she could allow herself to imagine happiness and what it might look like, without feeling the guilt that had previously assailed her at the prospect. In deep relaxation, that negative voice was stilled, giving positive expectations a chance to be experienced.

A Crucial Starting Point

This "follow-on" from the removal of trauma is vital in the case of clients who have experienced abuse in childhood, as there is likely much work to be done to find ways to manage deep-seated fear, anger, and loss of trust, as well as difficulty in handling strong feelings—something that indeed takes longer than the neutralising of trapped traumatic emotion. But very often, that work cannot even begin until the trauma has been dealt with. And that is why the rewind technique can offer such a crucial starting point in skilled hands.

item.title: Finding Compassion for Someone Who Hurt You
item.description:
Forgiveness

Finding Compassion for Someone Who Hurt You

Compassion, unlike forgiveness, lets your feelings soften toward one who hurt you.

Posted September 21, 2026

Meditating or visualizing a peaceful place can help cultivate compassion
Source: Johannes Plenio / pexels

Recently, someone I love hurt me. I don't understand why, and this person has withdrawn from all communication. The pain seems to vacillate with anger and self-pity. How could they do this to me?

Now the hurt of their abandonment has led me to think about how to move past the pain without locking the door for this person to return. I want repair to be possible. I’m holding out hope for that. So I'm starting by cultivating compassion.

Staying hurt and angry is exhausting. You know the feeling: You ruminate, replaying the words or the hurtful behavior over and over in your mind. The memory intrudes when you least expect it; your chest tightens, and you imagine what you wish you could say or do to the one who hurt you. Maybe you feel righteously angry; maybe you imagine retaliating. Then, perhaps, you cry.

This can go on for a long time—at which point you might start to worry that it's affecting your life, your mental health, or other relationships.

Compassion Isn’t the Same as Forgiveness

Holding compassion isn’t the same as forgiving. In Buddhist practice, compassion begins by recognizing that all beings share the exact same desire to be happy and avoid pain. Paired with wisdom, one wishes that all living beings may be free from suffering and its root causes.

Compassion may also be viewed as the recognition that the one who hurt you is a flawed, struggling human rather than a monster. That recognition lets your feelings soften toward them. Your lens shifts from focusing on the hurt they caused to seeing them as imperfect, wounded, or suffering. In contrast, forgiving is a decision you make, and this may (or may not) come later. I want to focus on compassion in this post.

Why Compassion Matters

Why is compassion important? Finding compassion helps you disentangle yourself from the other person. Holding on to the hurt or resentment has a way of keeping you tethered to the person who hurt you. You feel stuck and powerless. Finding compassion can help you loosen the grip.

It doesn’t erase the pain they caused, but it frees you from focusing on retaliation or trying fruitlessly to resolve the issue directly with them. Instead, the focus is on yourself and how you can free yourself from this hurt. It lets you reclaim your power over your mental health.

How to Find Compassion

Try to see the whole person. Widen your lens to see their strengths and your positive experiences with them.

When people behave badly, it's often because they're acting out of their own fear, insecurity, unresolved pain, ignorance, or exhaustion. They're shaped by their own history, limitations, and blind spots, as we all are. They may be reenacting a pattern from childhood, in a personal crisis, self-absorbed, or simply being careless. Often, they are unaware or unconscious of how their behavior affects others.

The point isn’t to make you feel sorry for them. And it doesn’t mean that their behavior is acceptable or that you invent a story that lets them get away with hurtful behavior. It just means recognizing that people are rarely as awful as their worst moments, even when that worst moment is the one that hurt you. Understanding a larger context, widening the lens on how you see them, can help calm the feelings of hurt or the “how could they do this to me?” loop.

Unfortunately, you can’t skip straight to compassion, as if you could flip that switch if you were a better person. You need time to grieve first. You need to name what you lost: trust, safety, time, or the kind of relationship you’d hoped for.

This might mean staying sad or mad for a while. You may still have fantasies of revenge or retaliation. Those voices in your mind may still try to script your comeback. If you don’t give yourself the time and space to grieve, the compassion collapses every time you are reminded of the one who hurt you, or what they did. Expressing the pain through journaling, artwork, or talk therapy can help.

What’s In It for You? The Upsides of Cultivating Compassion

Compassion often won’t get you the apology you think you deserve. Perhaps the person who hurt you doesn’t know or believe they did anything wrong, or they have just moved on. It is self-defeating to wait for them to realize how they hurt you.

Finding compassion means finding peace of mind, despite how they hurt you. It gives you back your power and lessens the power of their hurtful behavior or words.

Research has shown that when we feel compassion, our heart rate slows down, we secrete the “bonding hormone” oxytocin, and regions of the brain linked to empathy, caregiving, and feelings of pleasure light up, which often results in our wanting to approach and care for other people.

Make Compassion an Ongoing Practice

Compassion isn’t something you just claim once and hold. You may need to set an intention over and over, reminding yourself that we are all flawed, imperfect humans.

With self-awareness, catch yourself in the act of feeling hurt or angry, and interrupt the negative emotional loop. Remind yourself to widen that lens. Sometimes it helps to picture the other person as a wounded child, since we all carry our childhood wounds into adulthood. Don't forget to show compassion to yourself as you work through the hurt and anger.

It’s not quick or easy, but this is what healing means. Like a physical wound, healing takes time: The bleeding stops, then the wound begins to close. A scab forms, eventually turning into a scar that fades over time.

The Bottom Line

Finding compassion is about deciding that your own peace of mind is more important than the hurt. The compassion is for you, not for the other person. You can stay hurt or angry, or cultivate compassion. The truth is that finding compassion is often the harder choice. But it may be the one that actually frees you from the pain.

© Ann Gold Buscho, Ph.D. 2026

item.title: The Long Shadow of Silence in "This Much Is True"
item.description:
Sexual Abuse

The Long Shadow of Silence in "This Much Is True"

A new novel explores the lasting impact of staying silent about sexual assault.

Posted September 21, 2026

Katherine A. Sherbrooke
Source: lynne griffin

I recently spoke with Katherine A. Sherbrooke, author of the novel This Much is True, which explores the impact of remaining silent about past sexual assault on our current relationships.

Lynne: Your new novel, This Much is True, tackles a complicated issue in close relationships, primarily the lingering effects of sexual assault on a woman and her family. One of the themes you explore is the burden of silence over the years. Can you say more about that?

Katherine: The book places my main character, Veronica, who is in her 50s, in an impossible situation, when she shockingly realizes that the father of her daughter’s fiancé is the person who assaulted her in high school. Like many women, she chose at the time not to tell a soul—she even removed herself from the whole situation by dropping out of school and moving away.

But in the present, she can no longer avoid what once happened to her. She must either quietly accept her daughter's father-in-law into her family or speak up and possibly destroy her relationship with her daughter.

I was really interested in putting a fine point on the calculation every survivor must make, between the enormous cost of coming forward versus the heavy burden of staying silent.

L: I imagine your novel will resonate with far too many women given that according to the National Center for Victims of Crime, one in two women will experience physical sexual violence in their lifetime. And according to the Brennan Center for Justice, 80 percent of those cases go unreported. Can you tell us how you explored Veronica’s reasoning, and how your writing choices impacted her as she moved on with her life?

K: There is so much internalized shame for most survivors of assault. Add to that the burden borne by women who do choose to come forward. As Veronica says in the book, “it’s like shouting your most humiliating secret into a megaphone. Why would I do that?”

Yet silence comes with its own demands, which makes the bind doubly unfair. When we meet Veronica in the story, she’s happy, has a fulfilling career, a great marriage, and three well-adjusted adult children. Through the course of the book, she realizes that she's also been driven to keep an important part of herself hidden, even from her husband. Which to her, feels awfully close to living a lie.

L: Let’s talk about that. Veronica has a wonderful partner in her husband, Davis, but she’s never told him about the assault. Why do you think hiding this event, even from those we love, is so common?

Katherine: Part of staying silent, I think, is an understandable desire to make the trauma disappear. It can feel like the only chance a survivor has to erase it from their past. After all, once you speak the truth, you can’t take it back.

In this story, Veronica meets Davis not long after her assault. She is still trying to reclaim her self-worth and is worried he might think differently about her if he knew. While this is not necessarily a logical assumption, it is one that's easy to understand. The longer they are together, the more the version of herself she’s presented has solidified, which includes omitting this particular fact of her life. But when the perpetrator arrives at Veronica’s door, she needs her husband’s support more than anything, and her omission looms large.

This Much is True: A Novel
Source: Lynne Griffin

Lynne: Her omission also has an impact on her daughter. Tell us why you included that in your story.

Katherine: Yes, that’s an important part of this novel for both Veronica and her daughter Mara. One of the lingering impacts of the assault on Veronica is that it has made her an overly cautious mother, especially with her daughter. She feels ill-equipped to protect Mara from the kind of danger she herself experienced, and her constant warnings and caution signs have felt oppressive to her daughter, even insulting at some level, as if Veronica doesn’t trust Mara’s ability to make good choices.

This pattern creates a distance between them that may have been avoided had Veronica felt she could talk to her adult daughter about what happened to her. Sharing her experience, as hard as that would be, would certainly be more impactful on Mara than vague warnings. Not to mention how that kind of honesty might break open a new level of understanding between them as women.

Lynne: I don’t want to include any spoilers here, but I found the way you dealt with this dilemma deeply satisfying. How do you think Veronica changes over the course of the book and what might readers learn from that?

Katherine: Veronica realizes that she deserves to be free of this awful burden, that she deserves healing, and that real love is not conditional. She also stops questioning herself so much and starts to question instead the broken systems we have to deal with sexual assault. As she says, “the defendant is forced to defend, deflect, deny, all while the credibility of the victim is questioned.” It’s all a false promise and we need to find a better way through.

Veronica finds one, and I hope we as a society will start to shift our focus from questioning survivors, toward believing and protecting them, while making certain that the shame lands only where it really belongs.

item.title: Why I Say "Consensual Nonmonogamy" Instead of "Ethical Nonmonogamy"
item.description:
Polyamory

Why I Say "Consensual Nonmonogamy" Instead of "Ethical Nonmonogamy"

There are subtle differences between "consensual nonmonogamy" and "ethical nonmonogamy."

Posted September 21, 2026

Key points
  • "Consent" is an objective and behaviorally identifiable fact.
  • “Ethical” is hard to define and subjective, especially when applied to a diverse group of folks.
  • It’s very common for people to worry that they are doing nonmonogamy “wrong” by some set of outside standards.
Source: Ladanifer / Evanto

Recently, when I asked my audience what they wanted to know about non-monogamy, an interesting question came up: why do I use the term consensual non-monogamy (CNM), when many people use ethical non-monogamy (ENM) instead?

ENM and CNM mean essentially the same thing. They’re both umbrella terms that describe any relationship where partners agree, with informed consent, to have multiple romantic and/or sexual relationships. A huge range of relationship styles fit under this umbrella — everything from swinging, monogamish relationships, and open relationships that don’t involve romance to relationship anarchy, solo polyamory, and more.

Whether you use ENM or CNM, nobody is really going to be confused. If you don’t want to geek out on details of the language, you don’t have to, and I won’t argue with anyone who wants to use a different term than I choose. That said, there are subtle differences between the two terms, and contextual reasons why you might want to use one or the other.

Many clinicians, researchers, and scholars use CNM, whereas much of the public in open relationships use ENM. That makes sense to me, because the choice of which to use depends on context. Consider this: Consent (in this case, whether all parties know the relationship is open and have, at a minimum, willingness for that condition) is an objective and behaviorally identifiable fact. You can define it pretty clearly: Did all involved parties know and opt in? This makes consensual non-monogamy easy to describe and define, which is useful if you’re trying to do research or produce scholarly work.

It also makes sense that many people would want to use ethical non-monogamy to describe their own relationships. Most of us hope our relationships, whether open or not, have a lot more than consent going on: values-based decision-making, follow-through, enthusiastic endorsement, joyful participation, relational skill, and generous consideration of others. The term ethical non-monogamy implies an aspiration towards those values, which is a good thing.

At the same time, the very word “ethical” raises some questions. Whose definition of ethics are we using? What counts, and what doesn’t? Who gets to define whether any particular relationship counts as ethical? If my relationship doesn’t fit someone’s definition, is it then unethical? As a clinician, and as a person who trains clinicians, I’m not personally comfortable using terminology that implies that kind of judgement. “Ethical” is hard to define and subjective, especially when applied to a diverse group of folks.

It’s very common for people to worry that they are doing non-monogamy “wrong” by some set of outside standards, or to feel judged by others for having a different approach. Some things might fall outside of “ethical” for some people, but work just fine for others. As a relationship therapist, I can tell you that there’s no right or wrong way to do any relationship. Some things work better than others for most people, but there’s a wide range in terms of what’s possible.

For instance, imagine a setup in which one participant is willing to have a non-monogamous relationship, but not enthusiastic about it. Some might find that falls short of their sense of what’s ethical. For myself, I can certainly see some potential pitfalls with that setup, but it’s far from doomed. Even if the willingness is wobbly, at least everyone involved has the information they need to make decisions for themselves. I much prefer that to secret-keeping or gaslighting.

I’ve seen plenty of clearly unethical behavior in monogamous relationships, and I’ll bet you have too! I don’t believe that open relationships are more likely to be problematic than monogamy, and as a person in a polyamorous relationship myself, it’s important to me not to reinforce that idea. The truth is, when I’m training therapists, we’re usually discussing how to help when a relationship is struggling. We work with real human beings, in real (and sometimes messy) situations. That’s the nature of our work: What people aspire to isn’t always where they start.

As a trainer, my goal is to help fellow therapists work more effectively with relationships, whatever their starting point may be, and without making broad assumptions about how it must look in order to function well or be “good.” As a therapist, my goal is to help people build their relational skills, clarify and act in accordance with their values, and create relationships that are respectful, flexible, responsive to differences between individuals, and meaningful to the people within them. I do that for my clients no matter what label they use to describe their relationships.

item.title: Why a "Quiet Ego" Brings You Lasting Happiness
item.description:
Happiness

Why a "Quiet Ego" Brings You Lasting Happiness

A composed and observant inner voice can help you lead a fulfilling life.

Posted September 21, 2026

Key points
  • The quiet ego transcends egotism by steering one toward meaningful connections and personal development.
  • The first hallmark of a quiet ego is detached awareness, similar to the practice of mindfulness.
  • Nurturing the quiet ego amplifies one’s sense of compassion for oneself and others.
Source: Jeff Vinluan / Pexels

The concept of the “quiet ego” was introduced by Heidi A. Wayment and Jack J. Bauer, who describe it as a compassionate self-identity that counters a “noisy ego,” which refers to a more self-centered and potentially disruptive aspect of the self, driven by the need for validation, dominance, and constant attention.

A noisy ego is less attuned to the well-being of oneself and others and can drown out empathy, hinder personal development, and create discord in interpersonal relationships. In contrast, the quiet ego represents an interconnected worldview characterized by values promoting growth and a balance between self-compassion, personal agency, and concern for the welfare of others.

“The quiet ego constructs a self-identity that is neither excessively self-focused nor excessively other-focused—an identity that incorporates others without losing the self,” the authors write in their 2015 study.

The authors suggest that the quiet ego does not seek dominance or self-aggrandizement and transcends egotism by steering away from competitive self-centeredness toward meaningful connections and personal development. It empowers individuals to navigate life with heightened emotional intelligence, empathy, and resilience while focusing on sustained growth and well-being, both personally and collectively.

Here are the four defining values of a quiet ego, according to the authors.

  1. Detached awareness: The first hallmark of a quiet ego is detached awareness, similar to the practice of mindfulness. It involves observing oneself, others, and the environment without judgment or defensiveness. Compassionate and nonreactive observation of experiences allows individuals to relinquish control of the outcome of a situation and cultivate a deeper understanding of their emotions, thoughts, and behaviors without being overwhelmed or controlled by them.
  2. Inclusive identification: Inclusive identification refers to the extent to which an individual aligns themselves with others, perceiving similarities in personal qualities. It embodies a sense of connection and unity, fostering a mindset where the self is perceived as intertwined with a broader collective. A quieter ego displays cooperative tendencies and diminishes defensiveness when interacting with others, even those with whom one does not share similarities.
  3. Perspective-taking: Another essential trait of the quiet ego is the ability to empathize with others’ experiences and comprehend differing viewpoints without losing one's own identity. This characteristic promotes a sense of interconnectedness and compassion, fostering meaningful relationships and reducing conflict by accepting diverse perspectives. The quiet ego is flexible, open to new ideas, and willing to revise one's beliefs or opinions when presented with compelling evidence or differing viewpoints.
  4. Growth-mindedness: Growth-mindedness signifies a transformative shift from focusing on the need for personal gain and immediate gratification toward a broader perspective of long-term personal development and more intrinsically rewarding experiences. Crucially, growth-mindedness within the quiet ego extends beyond individual progress and values the growth of others. This includes acts of care and concern for the generations to come.

What Are the Benefits of a Quiet Ego?

Living by the values of the quiet ego can yield profound benefits in various aspects of life, including the following:

  • Psychological flourishing: A 2022 study found that quiet-ego-based interventions can enhance psychological flourishing, a state of optimal well-being, and overall thriving in life, by raising one’s emotional intelligence. Additionally, research shows that quiet ego characteristics are associated with greater resilience, improved coping skills, authenticity, and improved emotional regulation, which are linked to greater psychological well-being.
  • Improved social relationships: The quiet ego is associated with characteristics that improve the quality of one’s relationships. For instance, it encourages collaboration and effective communication in workplace settings and promotes deeper personal connections through empathy and perspective-taking. The quiet ego also boosts prosocial behavior by highlighting the benefits of giving and sharing with others and reducing excessive self-focus, which leads to experiencing greater well-being. Research shows that quieting the ego in group settings leads to feelings of stress relief, closeness, and greater self-development.
  • Personal growth: Researchers in the 2015 study highlight that the quiet ego is associated with qualities such as forgiveness, gratitude, humility, altruism, and reduced materialism. A 2022 study also found that a quiet ego is associated with greater clarity regarding one’s sense of self, which raises one’s self-esteem, resulting in personal growth.

Nurturing the quiet ego amplifies one’s sense of compassion for oneself and others. To begin with, it's vital to discern the sources of internal “noise,” question one’s dominant inner narratives, and identify areas where self-centeredness overshadows empathy or immediate gratification impedes long-term well-being. Embracing the quiet is a journey of self-reflection, a commitment to personal growth, openness, and empathy, as well as a pathway to a kinder world.

A version of this post also appears on Forbes.com.
