item.title: The Care That Might Have Helped Lindsay Clancy
item.description:
Postpartum Psychosis

The Care That Might Have Helped Lindsay Clancy

A psychiatric trial shows how different methods could have changed the outcome.

Posted September 21, 2026

Key points
  • The ODDESSI trial of Open Dialogue offers a vision of how Lindsay Clancy could have been better treated
  • OD works by offering immediate help, a continuous care team, and ongoing, patient-centered communication

“So you’re like a robot,” Lindsay Clancy’s attorney Kevin Reddington told Jennifer Tufts, the psychiatrist who treated Clancy. He was referring to Tufts’ repeated declarations of her own limited options—limited options on her computer files, on what went into her patient notes, and ultimately, based on her testimony, the care she gave.

As most people know by now, Clancy, in a state of postpartum distress, killed her three children with exercise bands. Then she attempted suicide. Her defense was postpartum psychosis: that she didn’t understand what she was doing that day in January 2023.

Clancy’s trial, which the Guardian called “America’s saddest murder trial,” ended in September 2026 with a hung jury.

Clancy had been prescribed 13 medications by half a dozen practitioners in a few months, checked herself into multiple hospitals, called suicide hotlines, all the while getting minimal to no help. Perhaps worse than the sheer number of medications, Clancy had frequent medication changes throughout, with drugs that can cause agitation and have withdrawal symptoms.

In court, Lindsay Clancy appeared like a figure in Greek tragedy—stiffly upright in the wheelchair she’s now confined to, dark hair streaming down her back. And a face that seemed both uncomfortably present and far, far away. Reddington, 75, with short white hair and a face that could have gone a few rounds in a boxing ring, was often filmed clutching Clancy's hand as she collapsed forward, weeping.

Lead prosecutor Jennifer Sprague argued Clancy knew what she was doing when she killed her children, and that she had gotten appropriate care. The hundreds of women who dressed in pink and surrounded the courtroom day after day to support Clancy begged to differ.

Knowing I watched and wrote about the trial, people have asked me how Clancy’s care before the crisis happened could have been different. Isn’t this just how it works? You have mental problems, you describe them to a doctor—briefly and often by telehealth, which Clancy did, though Reddington kind of charmingly called it “by television.”

Then you get prescriptions.

A recent study involving almost five hundred people, published in August of 2026 in medical mothership The Lancet, describes a treatment trial that sheds light on how this saddest of trials could have been different. Or possibly not been, at all.

The ODDESSI trial was the first large, randomized trial of the effectiveness of a mode of psychiatric care known as Open Dialogue. In the UK, ODDESSI was a controlled study, meaning researchers compared a group treated over two years with Open Dialogue methods with a group receiving standard care. Patients selected for the trial were, like Clancy, in psychiatric crisis.

Developed in Western Lapland, Finland, in the 1980s, Open Dialogue centers the patient and stresses immediate help, a continuous care team that stays with the patient throughout treatment, and ongoing communication that is patient-centered rather than top-down. As one practitioner puts it, clinicians bring “curiosity, uncertainty, and humility” to the process.

Doctors, the patient, and the patient’s family work together in frequent meetings, along with peer support. Rather than limited options, the group creates "a shared understanding of the problem, through a shared language."

The approach resembles Dorothea Buck’s trialogue. Patients are instrumental in charting their path to recovery. Medication is used by agreement of all concerned and isn’t considered primary.

In the ODDESSI trial, Open Dialogue participants had more than three‑times higher odds of never being admitted to psychiatric inpatient care, so far less hospitalization, and lower odds of re‑referral to crisis teams. In a webinar I attended, the study’s lead researcher, Russell Razzaque, announced Open Dialogue cut medication use, measured by cost, by one-quarter.

As important as these outcomes, Open Dialogue participants felt far more satisfied with their own lives. Their sense of the quality of their recovery, their quality of life and satisfaction with services received were much more positive than the controls’.

Lindsay Clancy received deeply fragmented care. At one point, two different practitioners prescribed for her without communicating with each other. She described what she was feeling to them, to suicide hotlines, to hospital staff. Almost no one involved shared their notes or sought out others’. Both Clancy’s husband and her mother knew she’d had intrusive thoughts about harming her children. Clancy’s clinicians remained unaware of this.

I can't imagine a case that needed a "shared language" more.

In testimony, Clancy’s caregivers seem to have asked few questions, certainly not probing questions. Instead, she received what I call checklist care: brief queries aimed at filling out the symptom lists that currently guide our practice. When Clancy reported that she felt suicidal, she was asked the textbook question of whether she “had a plan”—not the crucial question of what she imagined happening to her children if she died.

Open Dialogue isn’t a panacea. In the ODDESSI trial, OD didn’t change average time to relapse; it just greatly lowered the consequences of relapse.

Still, a Lindsay Clancy in Open Dialogue care would have seen the same people at every appointment. She would have avoided the chaotic, inappropriate medication she received, and had the emphasis correctly put on listening. Clancy’s husband and mother would have been part of the care team, sharing just how disturbing Lindsay's intrusive thoughts were.

Our current care is a late twentieth-century innovation, an attempt to leave behind Freudian thinking and stress the biology of mental states. Though biological theories, like low serotonin causing depression, have largely not panned out. Research like ODDESSI gives us a chance to correct again. Open Dialogue is resource-intensive, but it prevents the most expensive kind of care, hospitalization. And it has the potential to prevent tragedy.
